theme: Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 115. This psalm contrasts the living God with lifeless idols. Read it as the song of a small, exposed community in a land full of other gods.
settingTheScene: Psalm 115 was probably used in the second temple period. It begins with a famous line: “Not to us, O LORD.” The nations ask, “Where is their God?” That question could be asked of the returned exiles, a small people under Persian rule. The psalm’s answer is that God is in heaven and does as he pleases, while the gods of the nations are silver and gold, made by human hands.
observation: “Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory, for the sake of your steadfast love and your faithfulness!” (v. 1).
“Why should the nations say, Where is their God?” (v. 2).
“Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases” (v. 3).
“Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands” (v. 4).
“They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see” (v. 5).
“Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (v. 8).
“O Israel, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield” (v. 9).
“The heavens are the LORD’s heavens, but the earth he has given to the children of man” (v. 16).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with a humble prayer. “Not to us.” The people had just been through exile, return, and rebuilding, and they could easily have taken pride in their achievements. They deflect the glory. It belongs to God’s name, for the sake of his steadfast love and faithfulness.

The taunt of the nations is real: “Where is their God?” Israel has no king, no army, no visible image of their God. The answer is bold. Our God is in heaven and does whatever he pleases. He is not an object to be carried around. He is free and sovereign.

Then comes a sharp description of idols. They have mouths but cannot speak, eyes but cannot see, ears but cannot hear, noses but cannot smell, hands that cannot feel, feet that cannot walk. They are lifeless things dressed as persons. And the verdict in verse 8 is chilling: “Those who make them become like them.” What we worship shapes us. Whoever puts trust in something dead becomes deadened. Whoever worships power becomes hard; whoever worships money becomes cold. We become what we love.

The next section calls three groups to trust: Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD. Three times: “He is their help and their shield.” The refrain is a reminder that trust is a communal act.

The psalm closes with a blessing. “May the LORD give you increase, you and your children.” And with a promise of praise: “The dead do not praise the LORD… But we will bless the LORD from this time forth and forevermore.” Life is for praise.
connection: Isaiah 44:9-20 is a satirical description of idol-making. Romans 1:21-23 says people exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images. 1 John 5:21: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols.” 2 Corinthians 3:18: we are being transformed into the image of the Lord from one degree of glory to another. Colossians 3:5 says that covetousness is idolatry. John 8:50 shows Jesus seeking not his own glory.
application:
Ask what you might be becoming like. What do you give your attention and trust to most?

When you succeed at something, pray “Not to us, O LORD” before accepting the praise.

Identify one modern idol (money, image, comfort, control) and renounce it in prayer.
prayerPrompts: Give God the glory for something you were tempted to take credit for.
Ask him to bless those who trust him.
